items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A good that is both rivalrous and excludable"?
items.answer: private good
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of private good.

items.stem: Explain why the free-rider problem leads to the market failure of missing markets.
items.answer: Because non-payers cannot be excluded, people wait for others to pay; firms cannot earn revenue, so they do not produce the good at all even though society values it – the market is missing.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Because non-payers cannot be excluded, people wait for others to pay; firms cannot earn revenue, so they do not produce the good at all even though society values it – the market is missing. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Public goods are any goods provided by the government." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A public good is defined by non-rivalry and non-excludability; governments also provide private and merit goods such as healthcare and education, which are rival and excludable.
items.markingKey: A public good is defined by non-rivalry and non-excludability; governments also provide private and merit goods such as healthcare and education, which are rival and excludable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain whether the following is a public good: (i) a fireworks display over a harbour; (ii) a seat at a football match.
items.answer: (i) public good: everyone in the area can watch (non-rival) and non-payers cannot easily be excluded; (ii) private good: a seat is rival and tickets exclude non-payers.
items.markingKey: (i) public good: everyone in the area can watch (non-rival) and non-payers cannot easily be excluded; (ii) private good: a seat is rival and tickets exclude non-payers.

items.stem: Using the Thames Barrier in London as an example, explain public goods and government provision.
items.answer: Completed in 1982, the barrier protects around 1.4 million people from tidal flooding and is funded by the government. Flood protection benefits everyone in the area (non-rival) and no one can be excluded, so it would not be provided by the market; the government funds it through taxation.
items.markingKey: Context (Completed in 1982, the barrier protects around 1.4 million people from tidal flooding and is funded by the government.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Flood protection benefits everyone in the area (non-rival) and no one can be excluded, so it would not be provided by the market; the government funds it through taxation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to public goods and government provision.

items.stem: Explain, with real-world examples, why the free market fails to provide public goods and evaluate two ways in which governments can respond.
items.answer: Non-rivalry and non-excludability, free riding; examples: defence, street lighting, flood defences. Responses: direct provision funded by taxes (guarantees provision; risk of over/under-provision, opportunity cost); contracting out to private firms (efficiency, but monitoring costs).
items.markingKey: Non-rivalry and non-excludability, free riding; examples: defence, street lighting, flood defences. Responses: direct provision funded by taxes (guarantees provision; risk of over/under-provision, opportunity cost); contracting out to private firms (efficiency, but monitoring costs).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "non-excludability"?
options: The characteristic that it is impossible or very costly to prevent people who have not paid from using a good
The ability of a firm to influence the price of its product, which can lead to higher prices and lower output than in a competitive market
An action by the better-informed party to reveal information, such as offering a warranty or obtaining a qualification
A formal agreement between firms to fix prices or restrict output to act like a monopoly
items.answer: The characteristic that it is impossible or very costly to prevent people who have not paid from using a good
items.markingKey: A. "non-excludability" is the characteristic that it is impossible or very costly to prevent people who have not paid from using a good.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The characteristic that one person's consumption of a good does not reduce the amount available for others"?
items.answer: non-rivalry
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of non-rivalry.

items.stem: Distinguish between a quasi-public good and a public good.
items.answer: A pure public good is fully non-rival and non-excludable; a quasi-public good has these features only partly, e.g. roads become rival when congested and can be made excludable by tolls.
items.markingKey: A pure public good is fully non-rival and non-excludable; a quasi-public good has these features only partly, e.g. roads become rival when congested and can be made excludable by tolls. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Elena writes: "Because public goods are non-rivalrous, they cost nothing to produce." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Non-rivalry means one person's use does not reduce availability for others; public goods such as defence and flood barriers still use scarce resources and have opportunity costs.
items.markingKey: Non-rivalry means one person's use does not reduce availability for others; public goods such as defence and flood barriers still use scarce resources and have opportunity costs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that Government provision of public goods is likely to lead to government failure.
items.answer: There is a risk of government failure, but the alternative is no provision; careful appraisal and procurement reduce the risk.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: hard to know how much people value public goods; political motives may distort spending; lack of competition can cause inefficiency. Arguments against: without government, public goods are not provided at all; cost-benefit analysis can guide spending; competitive tendering improves efficiency. Supported judgement: There is a risk of government failure, but the alternative is no provision; careful appraisal and procurement reduce the risk. items.stem:
Read the source below.

A town of 10,000 households is considering a new flood wall costing $3 million. A survey suggests each household would be willing to pay $400 for the protection, but when the council asked for voluntary contributions only $600,000 was pledged.
— Hypothetical council report

Using the data, explain why the flood wall is under-provided without government action.
items.answer: Total willingness to pay = 10,000 × $400 = $4m > $3m cost, so the wall is worth building; but because households cannot be excluded from protection, many free ride and pledges ($0.6m) are far below the cost – the market fails.
items.markingKey: Total willingness to pay = 10,000 × $400 = $4m > $3m cost, so the wall is worth building; but because households cannot be excluded from protection, many free ride and pledges ($0.6m) are far below the cost – the market fails. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which of the following is the best example of adverse selection?
options: People with health problems are more likely to buy health insurance
Banks lend more after being bailed out
items.answer: People with health problems are more likely to buy health insurance
items.markingKey: A. Hidden characteristics before the transaction.

items.stem: "Moral hazard occurs when sellers lie about the quality of a product before it is sold." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: That is a hidden-characteristics problem (adverse selection); moral hazard is a change in behaviour after a transaction because the person is protected from the consequences.
items.markingKey: That is a hidden-characteristics problem (adverse selection); moral hazard is a change in behaviour after a transaction because the person is protected from the consequences. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "Moral hazard occurs when sellers lie about the quality of a product before it is sold." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: That is a hidden-characteristics problem (adverse selection); moral hazard is a change in behaviour after a transaction because the person is protected from the consequences.
items.markingKey: That is a hidden-characteristics problem (adverse selection); moral hazard is a change in behaviour after a transaction because the person is protected from the consequences. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the 2008 global financial crisis and explain what it reveals about asymmetric information and moral hazard.
items.answer: Banks sold mortgage-backed securities whose risks were poorly understood by buyers; when US house prices fell, losses spread worldwide and governments bailed out major banks. Originators knew more about loan quality than investors (adverse selection), and expectations of bailouts encouraged excessive risk-taking (moral hazard).
items.markingKey: Context (Banks sold mortgage-backed securities whose risks were poorly understood by buyers; when US house prices fell, losses spread worldwide and governments bailed out major banks.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Originators knew more about loan quality than investors (adverse selection), and expectations of bailouts encouraged excessive risk-taking (moral hazard). – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to asymmetric information and moral hazard.

items.stem: Explain how car-history reports and online seller ratings (e.g. on platforms such as Carousell or eBay) reduce asymmetric information.
items.answer: They give buyers verified information about past ownership, accidents and seller reliability, reducing adverse selection and allowing good-quality sellers to receive higher prices.
items.markingKey: They give buyers verified information about past ownership, accidents and seller reliability, reducing adverse selection and allowing good-quality sellers to receive higher prices.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Moral hazard makes deposit insurance and bank bailouts more harmful than beneficial.
items.answer: Insurance and bailouts create moral hazard, but their stabilising benefits are large; the answer is strong regulation rather than removing protection.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: encourages risky lending; taxpayers bear the cost. Arguments against: prevents bank runs and systemic collapse; costs of financial crises are enormous; regulation (capital requirements) limits moral hazard. Supported judgement: Insurance and bailouts create moral hazard, but their stabilising benefits are large; the answer is strong regulation rather than removing protection.

items.stem: A driver who has just bought comprehensive car insurance starts parking in unsafe areas. This is an example of which of the following?
items.answer: Moral hazard
items.markingKey: D. Behaviour changes after the contract because the cost of risk is borne by the insurer.

items.stem: Briefly explain why government bailouts of banks may create moral hazard.
items.answer: If banks expect to be rescued when they fail, they do not bear the full cost of risky lending, so they take more risks than they otherwise would.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If banks expect to be rescued when they fail, they do not bear the full cost of risky lending, so they take more risks than they otherwise would. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that Asymmetric information only affects buyers. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Either side can be less informed: insurers (sellers) know less about buyers' risks, while buyers of used cars know less than sellers.
items.markingKey: Either side can be less informed: insurers (sellers) know less about buyers' risks, while buyers of used cars know less than sellers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between signalling and screening.
items.answer: Signalling is action by the better-informed party to reveal information (warranties, qualifications); screening is action by the less-informed party to uncover it (inspections, medical examinations).
items.markingKey: Signalling is action by the better-informed party to reveal information (warranties, qualifications); screening is action by the less-informed party to uncover it (inspections, medical examinations). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: An insurance company introduces an excess (deductible) of $500 on claims. Explain how this reduces moral hazard.
items.answer: Policyholders now bear part of the cost of any claim, so they have an incentive to take care to avoid losses.
items.markingKey: Policyholders now bear part of the cost of any claim, so they have an incentive to take care to avoid losses.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

A used-car market contains 'good' cars worth $12,000 to buyers and 'lemons' worth $4,000. Buyers cannot tell them apart and believe half the cars are lemons. Owners of good cars will not sell for less than $10,000.
— Hypothetical example based on Akerlof (1970)

Using the data, explain what will happen in this market.
items.answer: Buyers offer the expected value 0.5 × 12,000 + 0.5 × 4,000 = $8,000; owners of good cars require $10,000, so they withdraw; only lemons remain, buyers then offer only $4,000 – adverse selection drives good cars out.
items.markingKey: Buyers offer the expected value 0.5 × 12,000 + 0.5 × 4,000 = $8,000; owners of good cars require $10,000, so they withdraw; only lemons remain, buyers then offer only $4,000 – adverse selection drives good cars out. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: In a market for used motorbikes, high-quality items are worth $20,000 to buyers and low-quality items (lemons) $4,000. Buyers cannot tell them apart and believe 50% are lemons. Sellers of high-quality items will not accept less than $16,000. Calculate the price buyers are willing to pay and explain whether high-quality items will be sold.
items.answer: $12000; high-quality items are not sold
items.markingKey: Expected value = 0.5 × 4,000 + 0.5 × 20,000 = 12000 [2]; < 16,000 so good sellers withdraw – adverse selection; average quality falls and the market may collapse to lemons [2].

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that government regulation is the best response to asymmetric information.
items.answer: Regulation is important in high-stakes markets (health, finance), but private signals and technology often address asymmetric information more cheaply.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: licensing, disclosure rules and consumer protection laws; mandatory insurance reduces adverse selection (health mandates). Arguments against: private solutions: warranties, reputation, ratings, certification; regulation can be costly and create barriers to entry; information technology is reducing asymmetries. Judgement: Regulation is important in high-stakes markets (health, finance), but private signals and technology often address asymmetric information more cheaply. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Using the example of health insurance, explain the difference between adverse selection and moral hazard and evaluate one policy to reduce each.
items.answer: Adverse selection: high-risk people more likely to buy – premiums rise, healthy people leave; policy: mandatory insurance (US Affordable Care Act mandate), community rating. Moral hazard: insured over-use services; policy: co-payments/excesses. Evaluate effectiveness, equity, costs.
items.markingKey: Adverse selection: high-risk people more likely to buy – premiums rise, healthy people leave; policy: mandatory insurance (US Affordable Care Act mandate), community rating. Moral hazard: insured over-use services; policy: co-payments/excesses. Evaluate effectiveness, equity, costs.

items.stem: Why is market power considered a market failure?
items.answer: Firms restrict output and raise price above marginal cost, causing allocative inefficiency
items.markingKey: Firms restrict output and raise price above marginal cost, causing allocative inefficiency. P > MC means output is below the allocatively efficient level.

items.stem: Tomás writes: "Large firms always harm consumers." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Large firms may achieve economies of scale and invest in R&D, lowering prices and improving products; harm arises when market power is abused (higher prices, less innovation).
items.markingKey: Large firms may achieve economies of scale and invest in R&D, lowering prices and improving products; harm arises when market power is abused (higher prices, less innovation). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the EU's €2.42 billion fine on Google in 2017, explain how it illustrates competition policy against abuse of market power.
items.answer: The European Commission found that Google had favoured its own comparison-shopping service in search results. Using dominance in search to disadvantage rivals reduced competition; the fine and required changes aimed to restore a level playing field.
items.markingKey: Context (The European Commission found that Google had favoured its own comparison-shopping service in search results.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Using dominance in search to disadvantage rivals reduced competition; the fine and required changes aimed to restore a level playing field. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to competition policy against abuse of market power.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Competition policy is the best way to deal with the market failure caused by market power."
items.answer: Competition policy is central, but regulation is needed for natural monopolies and international coordination for global firms.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: promotes competition, lowering prices and raising efficiency; deters cartels through large fines; blocks harmful mergers. Arguments against: natural monopolies need regulation, not competition; large fines may be treated as a cost of doing business; global tech firms are hard to regulate across borders; nationalisation or price caps may be needed in some industries. Supported judgement: Competition policy is central, but regulation is needed for natural monopolies and international coordination for global firms.

items.answer: Competition law prohibits anti-competitive behaviour such as cartels and abuse of dominance across the economy; regulation of a natural monopoly sets prices or quality standards for a single dominant firm where competition is not efficient.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate the welfare loss caused by market power compared with a competitive market, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: a monopolist's AR (demand) and MR, with MC. Profit-maximising output Qm where MC = MR, price Pm on AR. Competitive output Qc where P = MC (AR = MC) at Pc. Pm > Pc, Qm < Qc; welfare loss triangle between AR and MC from Qm to Qc; part of consumer surplus is transferred to the firm as abnormal profit.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: a monopolist's AR (demand) and MR, with MC. Profit-maximising output Qm where MC = MR, price Pm on AR. Competitive output Qc where P = MC (AR = MC) at Pc. Pm > Pc, Qm < Qc; welfare loss triangle between AR and MC from Qm to Qc; part of consumer surplus is transferred to the firm as abnormal profit. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: In 2016 the European Commission fined truck makers including Daimler, Volvo and DAF a total of €2.93 billion for a 14-year cartel. Explain how the cartel harmed customers.
items.answer: The firms coordinated prices and the timing of passing on emission-technology costs, so trucks were priced above competitive levels; customers (haulage firms) paid more, which also raised transport costs in the wider economy.
items.markingKey: The firms coordinated prices and the timing of passing on emission-technology costs, so trucks were priced above competitive levels; customers (haulage firms) paid more, which also raised transport costs in the wider economy.

items.stem: The market shares of the six largest mobile network operators are 22%, 18%, 16%, 15%, 14%, 4%. The second- and fourth-largest firms propose to merge. Calculate the CR4 before and after the merger and explain one reason the competition authority might block it.
items.answer: CR4 71% before, 85% after; merged firm 33%
items.markingKey: Before: 22 + 18 + 16 + 15 = 71% [1]; merged firm 18 + 15 = 33%, new top four 33 + 22 + 16 + 14 = 85% [2]; reason: greater market power → higher prices, less choice/innovation, risk of collusion [1].

items.stem:
Read the source below.

In the market for mobile phone services in a country, the largest four firms have market shares of 38%, 27%, 19% and 9%. The competition authority is reviewing a proposed merger between the second- and fourth-largest firms.
— Hypothetical competition authority report

Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio before the merger and explain why the authority may oppose the merger.
items.answer: CR4 = 38 + 27 + 19 + 9 = 93%; after the merger the new firm would have 36%, giving two firms with 74% between them; reduced competition could lead to higher prices and less choice and innovation.
items.markingKey: CR4 = 38 + 27 + 19 + 9 = 93%; after the merger the new firm would have 36%, giving two firms with 74% between them; reduced competition could lead to higher prices and less choice and innovation. items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that breaking up large technology firms is the best way to deal with their market power.
items.answer: Break-ups may be justified in extreme cases, but regulation of conduct is often a more practical first step.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "quasi-public good".
items.answer: A good that has some but not all characteristics of a public good, such as a road that is non-rival until congested

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "asymmetric information".
items.answer: A situation in which one party to a transaction has more or better information than the other, leading to market failure

items.stem: Distinguish between a merit good and a public good.
items.answer: A public good is defined by its characteristics (non-rival, non-excludable) and would not be provided by markets; a merit good (e.g. education) is rival and excludable but under-consumed because of positive externalities or imperfect information.
items.markingKey: A public good is defined by its characteristics (non-rival, non-excludable) and would not be provided by markets; a merit good (e.g. education) is rival and excludable but under-consumed because of positive externalities or imperfect information. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how licensing of professionals such as doctors addresses asymmetric information.
items.answer: Patients cannot judge medical competence; licensing requires minimum qualifications and standards, reducing the risk of poor-quality providers and giving consumers confidence.

items.stem: Briefly explain why monopolies may lead to allocative inefficiency.
items.answer: A monopolist maximises profit where MC = MR, which is below the competitive output; it sets price above marginal cost (P > MC), so consumers value extra units more than they cost to produce, but they are not produced – welfare loss.

items.answer: Adverse selection arises from hidden characteristics before a transaction (e.g. high-risk people buying insurance); moral hazard arises from hidden actions after a transaction (e.g. insured people taking more risks).

items.stem: "A high concentration ratio proves that firms are colluding." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Concentration shows that a few firms dominate, but it does not prove collusion; firms may compete fiercely (e.g. in price or innovation) even in concentrated markets.

items.stem: Street lights for a neighbourhood would cost $90,000. Each of the 2,000 households values it at $50. When asked to contribute voluntarily, only 30% of households pay their full valuation. Calculate total willingness to pay and the money raised, and explain why the good is not provided.
items.answer: Willingness to pay $100,000; raised $30,000; cost $90,000 – not provided because of free riding
items.markingKey: Total WTP = 2,000 × 50 = 100,000 > cost 90,000 [1]; raised = 30% × 2,000 × 50 = 30,000 [1]; raised < cost, so it is not provided [1]; households free ride because they cannot be excluded [1].

items.stem: Ana writes: "Asymmetric information only affects buyers." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Either side can be less informed: insurers (sellers) know less about buyers' risks, while buyers of used cars know less than sellers.
items.markingKey: Either side can be less informed: insurers (sellers) know less about buyers' risks, while buyers of used cars know less than sellers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the welfare loss caused by market power compared with a competitive market.
items.answer: Diagram: a monopolist's AR (demand) and MR, with MC. Profit-maximising output Qm where MC = MR, price Pm on AR. Competitive output Qc where P = MC (AR = MC) at Pc. Pm > Pc, Qm < Qc; welfare loss triangle between AR and MC from Qm to Qc; part of consumer surplus is transferred to the firm as abnormal profit.

Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline why public goods are not provided by the free market.
items.answer: Explain non-rivalry and non-excludability; a diagram can show the missing market: demand for the good (society's marginal benefit) is positive, but because individuals free ride, effective demand faced by firms is close to zero, so no output is produced although MSB > MSC for the first units. Government provision financed by taxes moves output to the optimum.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how adverse selection can cause under-consumption in a market such as health insurance.
items.answer: Diagram: market for insurance; with asymmetric information, insurers charge premiums based on average risk; low-risk buyers' demand falls (their MPB of insurance is below the premium), so demand shifts left from D (full information) to D1 and the quantity of insurance bought falls below the efficient level Q*. Welfare loss from under-provision; policy such as mandates shifts demand back.

items.stem: Briefly describe the EU's €2.42 billion fine on Google in 2017 and explain what it reveals about competition policy against abuse of market power.
items.answer: The European Commission found that Google had favoured its own comparison-shopping service in search results. Using dominance in search to disadvantage rivals reduced competition; the fine and required changes aimed to restore a level playing field.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Government regulation is the best response to asymmetric information.
items.answer: Regulation is important in high-stakes markets (health, finance), but private signals and technology often address asymmetric information more cheaply.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: licensing, disclosure rules and consumer protection laws; mandatory insurance reduces adverse selection (health mandates). Arguments against: private solutions: warranties, reputation, ratings, certification; regulation can be costly and create barriers to entry; information technology is reducing asymmetries. Supported judgement: Regulation is important in high-stakes markets (health, finance), but private signals and technology often address asymmetric information more cheaply.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that competition policy is the best way to deal with the market failure caused by market power.
items.answer: Competition policy is central, but regulation is needed for natural monopolies and international coordination for global firms.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: promotes competition, lowering prices and raising efficiency; deters cartels through large fines; blocks harmful mergers. Arguments against: natural monopolies need regulation, not competition; large fines may be treated as a cost of doing business; global tech firms are hard to regulate across borders; nationalisation or price caps may be needed in some industries. Judgement: Competition policy is central, but regulation is needed for natural monopolies and international coordination for global firms. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: To what extent is it true that Public goods must always be provided directly by the government?
items.answer: Governments must usually fund public goods, but they need not produce them directly; contracting out and new technology offer alternatives.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: free-rider problem prevents private provision; taxes ensure funding and universal access. Arguments against: government can contract private firms to build and operate them; technology can make some goods excludable (toll roads); philanthropy and community provision (Wikipedia, open-source software). Supported judgement: Governments must usually fund public goods, but they need not produce them directly; contracting out and new technology offer alternatives. items.stem: "Moral hazard makes deposit insurance and bank bailouts more harmful than beneficial." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Insurance and bailouts create moral hazard, but their stabilising benefits are large; the answer is strong regulation rather than removing protection.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: encourages risky lending; taxpayers bear the cost. items.stem: Why are public goods not provided by the free market?
options: They are too expensive to produce
Non-excludability leads to free riding, so firms cannot charge users
items.answer: Non-excludability leads to free riding, so firms cannot charge users
items.markingKey: C. With no way to exclude non-payers, there is no profit incentive.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "moral hazard"?
options: A situation where the party with better information before a transaction (hidden characteristics) is more likely to participate, such as high-risk people buying insurance
The share of total market output or sales accounted for by the largest firms, e.g. the four-firm concentration ratio (CR4)
An action by the better-informed party to reveal information, such as offering a warranty or obtaining a qualification
A situation where one party changes their behaviour after a transaction because they do not bear the full consequences, such as taking more risks after being insured
items.answer: A situation where one party changes their behaviour after a transaction because they do not bear the full consequences, such as taking more risks after being insured
items.markingKey: D. "moral hazard" is a situation where one party changes their behaviour after a transaction because they do not bear the full consequences, such as taking more risks after being insured.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "nationalisation"?
options: An action by the less-informed party to find out hidden information, such as medical checks before insurance
The share of total market output or sales accounted for by the largest firms, e.g. the four-firm concentration ratio (CR4)
An action by the better-informed party to reveal information, such as offering a warranty or obtaining a qualification
Transferring a privately owned firm into government ownership
items.answer: Transferring a privately owned firm into government ownership
items.markingKey: D. "nationalisation" is transferring a privately owned firm into government ownership.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a merit good and a public good.
items.answer: A public good is defined by its characteristics (non-rival, non-excludable) and would not be provided by markets; a merit good (e.g. education) is rival and excludable but under-consumed because of positive externalities or imperfect information.
items.markingKey: A public good is defined by its characteristics (non-rival, non-excludable) and would not be provided by markets; a merit good (e.g. education) is rival and excludable but under-consumed because of positive externalities or imperfect information. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between adverse selection and moral hazard.
items.answer: Adverse selection arises from hidden characteristics before a transaction (e.g. high-risk people buying insurance); moral hazard arises from hidden actions after a transaction (e.g. insured people taking more risks).
items.markingKey: Adverse selection arises from hidden characteristics before a transaction (e.g. high-risk people buying insurance); moral hazard arises from hidden actions after a transaction (e.g. insured people taking more risks). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why governments block some mergers.
items.answer: A merger can create a firm with significant market power that could raise prices, reduce choice and innovation; competition authorities assess whether the merger would substantially lessen competition.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A merger can create a firm with significant market power that could raise prices, reduce choice and innovation; competition authorities assess whether the merger would substantially lessen competition. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a public good and a quasi-public good.
items.answer: A pure public good is fully non-rival and non-excludable; a quasi-public good has these features only partly, e.g. roads become rival when congested and can be made excludable by tolls.
items.markingKey: A pure public good is fully non-rival and non-excludable; a quasi-public good has these features only partly, e.g. roads become rival when congested and can be made excludable by tolls. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between signalling and screening.
items.answer: Signalling is action by the better-informed party to reveal information (warranties, qualifications); screening is action by the less-informed party to uncover it (inspections, medical examinations).
items.markingKey: Signalling is action by the better-informed party to reveal information (warranties, qualifications); screening is action by the less-informed party to uncover it (inspections, medical examinations). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a firm's market share and a four-firm concentration ratio.
items.answer: Market share is one firm's share of total sales; the CR4 is the combined share of the four largest firms, indicating how concentrated the market is.
items.markingKey: Market share is one firm's share of total sales; the CR4 is the combined share of the four largest firms, indicating how concentrated the market is. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to the 2008 global financial crisis, explain how it illustrates asymmetric information and moral hazard.
items.answer: Banks sold mortgage-backed securities whose risks were poorly understood by buyers; when US house prices fell, losses spread worldwide and governments bailed out major banks. Originators knew more about loan quality than investors (adverse selection), and expectations of bailouts encouraged excessive risk-taking (moral hazard).
items.markingKey: Context (Banks sold mortgage-backed securities whose risks were poorly understood by buyers; when US house prices fell, losses spread worldwide and governments bailed out major banks.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Originators knew more about loan quality than investors (adverse selection), and expectations of bailouts encouraged excessive risk-taking (moral hazard). – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to asymmetric information and moral hazard.

items.stem: The market shares of the six largest banks are 24%, 17%, 12%, 10%, 8%, 6%. The second- and fourth-largest firms propose to merge. Calculate the CR4 before and after the merger and explain one reason the competition authority might block it.
items.answer: CR4 63% before, 71% after; merged firm 27%
